title: ML Evaluation Metrics: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on classification and regression metrics, from the confusion matrix through ROC/AUC and regression errors, plus handling class imbalance. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Confusion Matrix and Core Metrics
points: Confusion matrix is a 2x2 table of actual vs predicted: TP, FP, FN, TN; FP is a Type I error and FN is a Type II error
Accuracy = (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN): the share of all predictions that are correct
Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of everything predicted positive, how much was right; use it when false alarms are costly (spam filter)
Recall (sensitivity, TPR) = TP/(TP+FN): of all real positives, how many were found; use it when misses are costly (cancer screening)
Worked example: TP=40, FP=10, FN=20, TN=930 gives accuracy 97%, precision 80%, recall 66.7%

chapters.title: F1 Score and the Threshold Trade-off
points: F1 = 2PR/(P+R): the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which punishes a big gap between them (P=1.0, R=0.1 gives F1≈0.18, not 0.55)
Raising the decision threshold (default 0.5) raises precision and lowers recall; lowering it does the reverse
F-beta = (1+β²)PR/(β²P+R): β=2 weights recall more, β=0.5 weights precision more
Macro F1 averages classes equally; micro F1 pools all counts (equals accuracy in single-label multiclass); weighted F1 averages by class support
sklearn: precision_recall_fscore_support(y_true, y_pred) and classification_report(y_true, y_pred) print all of these per class

chapters.title: ROC Curve and AUC
points: ROC curve plots TPR (y) against FPR = FP/(FP+TN) (x) as the threshold sweeps from 1 to 0
AUC is the area under the ROC curve; it equals the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative
AUC 0.5 means random guessing (the diagonal) and 1.0 means perfect ranking; below 0.5 means the labels are inverted
AUC is threshold-independent and measures ranking only; it says nothing about calibration or the best cutoff
On heavy imbalance ROC/AUC looks optimistic because the huge TN count keeps FPR tiny; use the precision-recall curve and average precision (PR-AUC) instead
sklearn: roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score) needs probabilities or scores, never hard 0/1 labels

chapters.title: Regression Metrics: MAE, RMSE, R2
points: MAE = mean(|y−ŷ|): average error in the target's own units, robust to outliers
MSE = mean((y−ŷ)²) and RMSE = √MSE: squaring penalizes large errors heavily, so RMSE ≥ MAE and a large gap signals outliers
R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot: the share of variance explained; 0 equals predicting the mean, and it can go negative on test data for a bad model
Adding features never lowers training R²; use adjusted R² to penalize useless features
Choose MAE when all errors cost the same, RMSE when big misses are disproportionately bad; for example y=[3,5,7], ŷ=[2,5,10] gives MAE=1.33 and RMSE=1.83

chapters.title: Class Imbalance and How to Handle It
points: A model that always predicts the majority class scores 99% accuracy on a 1% positive dataset, so judge with recall, precision, F1 and PR-AUC
Use stratified splits (train_test_split(..., stratify=y), StratifiedKFold) so every fold keeps the class ratio
Class weights: class_weight='balanced' in sklearn or scale_pos_weight in XGBoost raises the loss on minority errors with no data change
Resample the training set only: random oversampling, undersampling, or SMOTE (imblearn) which interpolates new minority points
Resampling before the train/test split leaks synthetic copies into the test set and inflates scores; resample inside the CV pipeline
Tune the decision threshold on a validation set instead of using 0.5; it is often the cheapest fix

chapters.title: Metrics Cheat Sheet
points: Formulas: Acc=(TP+TN)/N, P=TP/(TP+FP), R=TP/(TP+FN), F1=2PR/(P+R), FPR=FP/(FP+TN)
Pick by cost: false alarms hurt → precision; misses hurt → recall; need balance → F1; ranking quality → AUC
Imbalanced data: ignore accuracy, use PR-AUC/F1, stratify, class weights, tune the threshold
Regression: MAE for typical error, RMSE to punish outliers, R² for variance explained (can be negative)
Never resample before splitting; never feed hard labels to roc_auc_score; always report the threshold used
